html:
A treaty signed in 1899 between the Crown and First Nations around Lesser Slave Lake, later joined by others, covering northern Alberta, northwestern Saskatchewan, northeastern British Columbia and the southern Northwest Territories. By area it is the largest of the Numbered Treaties of Canada.

Canada made it after the Klondike gold rush sent thousands of prospectors through the region. The signers were Cree and Dene peoples, among them the Dënesųłiné, Dene Tha' and Dane-zaa (Beaver). The Métis were offered scrip, a one-time grant of land or money, instead.

The written text says the nations gave up their land for reserves, yearly payments and the right to keep hunting, trapping and fishing. Elders remember a promise of peace and friendship, with no surrender of land. That gap has fed a century of disputes, sharpened because the Alberta oil sands lie inside Treaty 8. The Akaitcho Dene still argue they never ceded their land.
